turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. ____. I'm, well, I'm here because I'm just struggling so much at work lately, and it's getting to the point where I'm genuinely terrified I'm going to make a huge mistake. I'm a registered nurse, and I've been doing this for a while, so I should be used to the chaos, but it feels like my brain just cannot filter anything out anymore. The main reason I finally made this appointment is that on the floor, I lose my train of thought constantly. And I mean constantly. It's like, I'll be in the middle of charting or figuring out a complex patient flow issue, trying to mentally organize who needs to go to CT and who needs meds, and then... an IV pump beeps down the hall. Or I hear one of the other nurses asking a tech a question, or a call light goes off in a room that isn't even mine, and suddenly, poof. Whatever I was working on is just completely gone from my head. I have to stand there for what feels like five minutes just staring blankly, trying to retrace my mental steps to figure out what I was doing right before the beep. It's exhausting, honestly, and it's making me so incredibly anxious because in nursing, you can't just forget things like that. You just can't.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as IV pumps beeping, other nurses talking, or call lights going off, which causes them to lose their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient describes their mind going blank ('completely gone from my head', 'staring blankly') and having difficulty sustaining concentration on complex tasks due to the distractions.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had these kinds of attention and distractibility problems since you were a child?
turns.patient_response: Oh, wow, yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my mom about this the other day, well, maybe not the other day, maybe a couple of weeks ago, when I first started thinking I needed to see someone. She was cleaning out her attic and found all these old report cards from elementary school, like, third and fourth grade, and she was reading the teacher comments to me over the phone. And it was honestly kind of shocking how consistent it was. Every single teacher wrote almost the exact same thing: "She's very bright, but she's so careless." Or, "She has so much potential, but she's always losing her worksheets." And it's true, I would literally do the homework, put it in my folder, and then by the time I got to school, it was just... gone. Or I'd forget to take it out of my backpack. I remember my mom used to get so frustrated with me, bless her heart, because she would have to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night, literally right next to me, just to make sure I actually finished an assignment and put it in the right place. If she walked away to stir a pot on the stove, I'd be staring out the window or picking at the eraser on my pencil, completely forgetting what I was supposed to be doing. So, yes, it's definitely been there since I was little, it just feels like now, with the stakes being so much higher at the hospital, I can't just rely on my mom to sit next to me and keep me on track, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that her elementary school teachers consistently noted she was 'so careless' in her work.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on homework, requiring her mother to sit next to her every night to keep her on track.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient notes she would fail to finish assignments unless her mother sat right next to her to ensure completion.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states she was 'always losing her worksheets' and that completed homework would frequently go missing before she got to school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by staring out the window or picking at an eraser the moment her mother stepped away.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions forgetting to take homework out of her backpack and completely forgetting what she was supposed to be doing.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself worrying about many different things most days, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?
turns.patient_response:
Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm just sitting around worrying about random things or, like, inventing problems in my head when everything is fine. It's more that I'm stressed about the things that are actually happening, you know? Like work. I'm definitely stressed about work, but that's because there *is* an immediate problem—the fact that I can't seem to hold a thought in my head for more than ten seconds without getting derailed. 

Like, if I'm at home on my day off and I don't have any major chores hanging over my head—which is rare, because I always put off doing laundry until I'm literally out of scrubs—but if I actually have a free day, I'm not sitting on the couch agonizing about, I don't know, the economy or what my neighbor thinks of me or some vague sense of doom. I'm usually just trying to figure out what I wanted to do that day, and then I end up starting a movie, pausing it to go get a snack, noticing the fridge needs wiping down, and then three hours later I'm reorganizing my Tupperware cabinet and the movie is still paused. But I'm not *worried* during that. I'm just... scattered. 

The anxiety I feel is very specific to the fact that I know I'm dropping the ball. It's like this constant, heavy feeling in my chest when I'm at the hospital because I know, factually, that my brain is not cooperating, and I'm terrified of the consequences of that. But it's not a general, everyday worry about everything under the sun. It's very tied to my actual performance and my fear of messing up a patient's care because I got distracted by a monitor beeping three rooms down. So, no, I don't think I'm a worrier in the way you're describing. I just have very real, very pressing reasons to be stressed right now.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on leisure activities, such as starting a movie but abandoning it to do unrelated tasks for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions getting derailed from thoughts in seconds and being distracted by extraneous stimuli, like a monitor beeping three rooms down.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies having general, everyday worry about various things, stating their stress is strictly tied to actual performance issues and not generalized anxiety.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel restless or like you have to keep moving, even when you’re supposed to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Restless? Like having to keep moving? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, as a nurse, I'm on my feet for twelve hours a shift, so I'm always moving anyway. But it's not like a compulsion or this internal motor driving me, you know? It's just the nature of the job. 

When I actually do get a chance to sit down—like if I'm at the nurses' station finally trying to catch up on my charting, assuming I haven't been pulled away by a bed alarm or a doctor needing something—I can sit still just fine. Physically, anyway. My body isn't the problem. I don't feel like I need to tap my foot or bounce my leg or get up and pace the halls. I'm usually so exhausted by the time I get to sit that I'm more than happy to just stay in the chair. 

It's really just my brain that won't sit still. Like I was saying before, I'll be sitting perfectly quietly, staring at the computer screen, and my mind is just jumping from the charting to the beep down the hall to whether or not room 412 got their pain meds yet, and then I realize I've been sitting there for five minutes and haven't typed a single word. But physically? No, I don't get that restless, jumpy feeling. If I go to a movie or a long meeting, I'm not the person squirming in their seat. I might completely zone out and miss half of what was said, but I'll be sitting perfectly still while I do it. So no, the physical restlessness isn't really something I deal with.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes their mind jumping to extraneous stimuli like a beep down the hall or unrelated thoughts while trying to work.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies needing to tap their foot, bounce their leg, or squirm in their seat.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states they can sit still just fine and do not feel the need to get up and pace.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies experiencing physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient denies feeling like they are driven by an internal motor.

turns.doctor_question: Do these concentration problems happen in more than one setting, like at work and at home?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, oh gosh, yes. It's everywhere. It's honestly exhausting because there's no escape from it. Like I was saying about work, it's a nightmare trying to chart or keep track of orders, but then I come home and it's not like my brain suddenly switches gears and works normally. It's the exact same thing, just with different tasks. 

Like, my apartment is... well, it's a disaster zone right now, to be perfectly honest. I'll walk in the door after a shift, completely drained, and I'll think, "Okay, I just need to pay this one electric bill before I forget." So I go to my desk, but on the way, I see a pile of mail on the kitchen counter. I start sorting through the mail, and I find a coupon for that new Thai place down the street. That makes me realize I'm starving, so I open the fridge to see what I can make. The fridge is practically empty, except for some questionable leftovers, which reminds me I meant to take the trash out this morning. So I grab the trash bag, take it out to the dumpster, and on my way back in, I check my phone and see a text from my sister that I forgot to reply to yesterday. I sit on the couch to text her back, and then... I don't know, an hour goes by, I'm scrolling through social media, I haven't eaten, the mail is still half-sorted on the counter, and I completely forgot about the electric bill. It's like that every single day. 

And it affects my relationships, too. If I'm out to dinner with a friend, I want to listen to them, I really do, but if the restaurant is loud or there's a TV playing sports in the background, or even just people walking past our table, I find myself completely losing the thread of the conversation. I'll realize my friend just asked me a question and I have absolutely no idea what she was talking about for the last five minutes. It's so embarrassing to have to ask people to repeat themselves constantly, or to just nod and smile and hope I'm agreeing to the right thing. 

So it's definitely not just a work problem. It's work, it's home, it's socializing, it's running errands... it's literally every aspect of my life. I can't think of a single setting where I don't struggle with this. It just feels like my brain is a sieve, no matter where I am or what I'm trying to do.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes losing the thread of conversations and being unable to sustain focus on a single task at home.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits to realizing a friend just asked a question and having no idea what they were talking about for the last five minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes starting multiple tasks at home (paying a bill, sorting mail) but failing to follow through and finish them.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states their apartment is a 'disaster zone,' indicating difficulty organizing their living space and tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily sidetracked by extraneous stimuli, such as a TV playing, people walking by, or seeing unrelated items around the house.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly mentions forgetting to pay an electric bill and forgetting to reply to a text message.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also often lose things you need, like keys, your phone, or important paperwork?
turns.patient_response:
Lose things? Actually, no. That’s one of the few things I feel like I actually have a handle on, surprisingly enough. I know it sounds like I should, given everything else I just told you about my apartment being a disaster and my brain jumping around, but I really don't lose my physical items. 

Like my keys, for example. I have this very specific routine because I know if I don't do it, I'll be in trouble. I have this blue ceramic bowl right by the front door—my aunt actually brought it back for me from a trip to Oaxaca a few years ago, it's really pretty—and the absolute very second I walk through the door, the keys go into the bowl. Every single time. It's practically muscle memory at this point. 

And my phone? My phone is basically an extension of my body. It's either in my hand, in my purse, or shoved deep into my scrub pocket. You really learn to keep track of your devices as a nurse. At the hospital, we have these Ascom phones we have to carry around for our shifts, and it is a massive ordeal if you lose one of those—they cost a fortune, and nursing management will literally hunt you down. So I'm always doing this little pat-down check: keys, phone, badge, wallet. 

As for paperwork, I mean, I have a specific drawer for it. Now, if you were to open that drawer, is it a beautifully color-coded filing system? Absolutely not. It’s a completely chaotic mountain of unsorted envelopes, old utility bills, and medical journals I swear I’m going to read someday. But the important paperwork itself isn't *lost*, you know? I know exactly which chaotic pile it’s sitting in. 

So, no, I'm not the person tearing the couch cushions apart looking for my car keys while I'm running twenty minutes late. I might be running late because I got distracted wiping down the baseboards instead of putting my shoes on, but when I finally do go to leave, I know exactly where my keys are. I guess I just overcompensated in that one specific area of my life so I wouldn't totally fall apart. But yeah, losing things isn't really an issue for me.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes her apartment as a 'disaster' and her paperwork drawer as a 'completely chaotic mountain of unsorted envelopes,' indicating difficulty keeping belongings in order.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states she does not lose physical items like keys, phones, or paperwork, noting she has a handle on this area.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions her 'brain jumping around' and gives an example of getting distracted by wiping down baseboards instead of putting on her shoes.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often interrupt people or blurt out answers before they finish asking the question?
turns.patient_response:
Interrupting? Um, no. No, I really don't think I do that. If anything, I'm kind of the exact opposite? 

Because, like I was saying earlier about losing the thread of conversations, I'm usually so focused on just trying to hold onto the words coming out of someone's mouth that I don't even have a response formulated yet. It's like my brain has this... this lag time, I guess you could call it. So blurting things out isn't really my issue at all. I mean, my best friend Sarah—we've been friends since nursing school, actually, we survived our med-surg clinicals together which is a bonding experience like no other—she's the one who talks a mile a minute and constantly talks over people. I love her, but she's definitely an interrupter. I'm always the sounding board in the relationship. I just sit there and let people talk. 

And it's the same way at work. Sometimes a patient will be telling me this long, incredibly elaborate story—like, I'll ask a simple question about whether they have any drug allergies, and suddenly they're giving me their entire medical history starting from a knee surgery they had in 1994, including what they had for breakfast that morning and their opinions on the hospital food. And I just stand there and nod. I don't cut them off. I probably *should* cut them off, honestly, because we have so little time on the floor and I usually have three other patients waiting for their meds or needing to use the bathroom, but I just... I don't have that impulse to jump in and stop them. I just let them talk while my brain is secretly off somewhere else, wondering if the pharmacy ever tubed up the IV antibiotics for room 410. 

Even with the doctors, when they're giving orders or explaining a care plan, I'm just quietly listening—or trying to listen, anyway. I never jump in and finish their sentences. I know some people get really eager to share their thoughts or they just know what the other person is going to say so they blurt it out, but I'm usually just trying to process the first half of their sentence while they're already on the second half. So, no, talking over people or blurting out answers? That's really not me. I'm much more likely to just be totally quiet and then realize way too late that I was supposed to actually answer a question they asked me two minutes ago.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes her mind wandering while people are speaking directly to her, causing her to miss questions and realize too late that she was supposed to answer.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting out answers, stating she never jumps in to finish people's sentences.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting others, noting she is the 'exact opposite' and just lets people talk without cutting them off.
